moments.title: Can we stop apologizing for not knowing about money
moments.summary: The speaker opens with the phrases she hears constantly — I don't know too much about investing, I'm really bad with numbers, I'm sorry but this is a silly question — and says the apology treats not knowing finance as a measure of how capable we are.
moments.evidence: I don't know too much about investing. I'm really bad with numbers. I'm sorry, but this is a really silly question.

moments.title: We were taught math, science, even baking — but not how to invest
moments.summary: The argument for why the apology is misplaced: not knowing something you were never taught is not a failure.
moments.evidence: We were taught math, science, even baking. But we weren't taught how to invest. Not knowing something you were never taught is not a failure.

moments.title: Ask the stupid question, and ask again
moments.summary: She tells the viewer not to pretend to understand out of fear of judgement, to ask the question and ask again, because confidence comes from knowing you can learn rather than from knowing everything.
moments.evidence: Ask the question. Ask the stupid question. And if you don't understand it, ask again. Because confidence doesn't come from knowing everything. It comes from knowing that you can learn.

moments.title: No judgment, no jargon, no embarrassment
moments.summary: She names that as what Investing for Mummies is trying to be: a space where you can say you don't know and ask to be taught.
moments.evidence: No judgment, no jargon, no embarrassment. Just a safe space for you to say, I don't know, teach me.
